questions.question: A car travels 90 miles in 5 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 90 / 5 = 18 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: A car travels 240 miles in 5 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 240 / 5 = 48 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: A car travels 240 miles in 4 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 240 / 4 = 60 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: A car travels 150 miles in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 150 / 3 = 50 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: A car travels 180 miles in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 180 / 3 = 60 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: A car travels 198 miles in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 198 / 3 = 66 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: A car travels 60 miles in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance over time: 60 / 2 = 30 miles per hour.
questions.memoryHook: Speed is distance divided by time.

questions.question: An object moves at 30 meters per second for 5 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 30 times 5 = 150 meters.

questions.question: An object moves at 10 meters per second for 3 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 10 times 3 = 30 meters.

questions.question: An object moves at 20 meters per second for 3 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 20 times 3 = 60 meters.

questions.question: An object moves at 10 meters per second for 5 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 10 times 5 = 50 meters.

questions.question: An object moves at 40 meters per second for 5 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 40 times 5 = 200 meters.

questions.question: An object moves at 10 meters per second for 4 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 10 times 4 = 40 meters.

questions.question: An object moves at 50 meters per second for 5 seconds. How far does it travel?
questions.explanation: Distance is speed times time: 50 times 5 = 250 meters.

questions.question: An object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared for 5 seconds, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Final speed is acceleration times time: 2 times 5 = 10 meters per second.
questions.memoryHook: Speed change is acceleration times time.

questions.question: An object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared for 4 seconds, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Final speed is acceleration times time: 2 times 4 = 8 meters per second.
questions.memoryHook: Speed change is acceleration times time.

questions.question: An object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared for 3 seconds, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Final speed is acceleration times time: 2 times 3 = 6 meters per second.
questions.memoryHook: Speed change is acceleration times time.

questions.question: An object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared for 6 seconds, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Final speed is acceleration times time: 2 times 6 = 12 meters per second.
questions.memoryHook: Speed change is acceleration times time.

questions.question: An object accelerates at 3 meters per second squared for 5 seconds, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Final speed is acceleration times time: 3 times 5 = 15 meters per second.
questions.memoryHook: Speed change is acceleration times time.

questions.question: An object accelerates at 5 meters per second squared for 6 seconds, starting from rest. What is its final speed?
questions.explanation: Final speed is acceleration times time: 5 times 6 = 30 meters per second.
questions.memoryHook: Speed change is acceleration times time.

questions.question: A 4 kg object accelerates at 3 meters per second squared. What force is acting on it?
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration: 4 times 3 = 12 newtons.

questions.question: A 2 kg object accelerates at 5 meters per second squared. What force is acting on it?
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration: 2 times 5 = 10 newtons.

questions.question: A 4 kg object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared. What force is acting on it?
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration: 4 times 2 = 8 newtons.

questions.question: A 6 kg object accelerates at 3 meters per second squared. What force is acting on it?
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration: 6 times 3 = 18 newtons.

questions.question: A 2 kg object accelerates at 2 meters per second squared. What force is acting on it?
questions.explanation: Force is mass times acceleration: 2 times 2 = 4 newtons.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: The newton is named for Isaac Newton; one newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 meter per second squared (1 N = 1 kg x m/s^2).

questions.question: What is Newton's first law also called?
distractors: The law of action and reaction
questions.explanation: Inertia is an object's resistance to changing its motion, so the first law - objects keep their state of motion unless a force acts - is named after it.

questions.question: What does Newton's first law state?
questions.correctAnswer: An object stays at rest or in motion unless a force acts on it
distractors: Every action has an equal reaction
questions.explanation: A puck sliding on ice keeps gliding because almost no friction acts on it; without a force, its motion would not change at all.
questions.memoryHook: Objects keep doing what they are doing.

questions.question: What is Newton's second law?
questions.explanation: Written as F = m x a: double the mass needs double the force to get the same acceleration.

questions.question: What is Newton's third law?
questions.correctAnswer: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
questions.explanation: When a rocket pushes exhaust gas downward, the gas pushes the rocket upward - the paired forces act on different objects.

questions.question: What force pulls objects toward Earth?
questions.explanation: Gravity is the attraction between masses; Earth's huge mass pulls everything near it toward Earth's center.

questions.question: What is friction?
questions.correctAnswer: A force that opposes motion between surfaces
distractors: A force that pulls objects down
A force that pushes objects apart
questions.explanation: Friction comes from microscopic roughness where surfaces touch, which is why rough shoe soles grip the ground and smooth ice does not.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of energy?
questions.explanation: The joule is named for James Joule; lifting a small apple by about one meter takes roughly one joule of energy.

questions.question: What is kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Any moving object has it - a rolling ball, flowing water, or moving air - and heavier or faster objects carry more of it.

questions.question: What is potential energy?
questions.explanation: It is energy waiting to be released, like water held behind a dam or a stretched rubber band.

questions.question: What is gravitational potential energy?
questions.correctAnswer: Energy stored by an object's height above the ground
questions.explanation: The higher an object is lifted, the more work was done against gravity to raise it, so the more energy is stored - it grows with both mass and height.

questions.question: What happens to kinetic energy when speed doubles?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling speed quadruples it.

questions.question: What is the law of conservation of energy?
questions.correctAnswer: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed in form
distractors: Energy only comes from the Sun
questions.explanation: A swinging pendulum trades potential energy and kinetic energy back and forth, but the total amount never changes.

questions.question: What is work in physics?
questions.correctAnswer: Force times distance moved in the direction of the force
questions.explanation: No movement means no work: pushing on a wall that does not move does zero work, however hard you push, because the distance is zero.

questions.question: What is power?
questions.correctAnswer: The rate at which work is done
questions.explanation: Power is work divided by time.
questions.memoryHook: Power is how fast work happens.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of power?
questions.explanation: The watt is named for James Watt; a 100-watt bulb uses 100 joules of energy every second it is on.

questions.question: What is the speed of light in a vacuum?
questions.explanation: That is about 3 x 10^8 meters per second - fast enough to circle Earth about seven and a half times in a single second.

questions.question: What type of wave is light?
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic waves are vibrating electric and magnetic fields; unlike sound, they need no material to travel through and can cross empty space.

questions.question: What type of wave is sound?
questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium, so it is a mechanical wave.
questions.memoryHook: Sound needs something to travel through.

questions.question: What is the frequency of a wave?
questions.correctAnswer: The number of waves that pass a point each second
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz): a frequency of 10 Hz means 10 complete waves pass the point every second.

questions.question: What is wavelength?
questions.correctAnswer: The distance between two matching points on a wave
distractors: The number of waves per second
questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next.

questions.question: What is amplitude?
questions.correctAnswer: The height of a wave from its center line
distractors: The number of waves per second
questions.explanation: Larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy - for a sound wave, a bigger amplitude sounds louder.

questions.question: What happens when light passes through a prism?
questions.explanation: Each color bends by a slightly different amount inside the glass, so white light fans out into a spectrum of colors.

questions.question: What is reflection?
questions.explanation: Mirrors and calm water reflect light predictably: the angle at which light arrives equals the angle at which it bounces away.

questions.question: What is refraction?
questions.correctAnswer: Light bending as it passes from one medium to another
questions.explanation: Light changes speed when it enters a new medium, and that speed change bends its path - which is why a straw looks broken in a glass of water.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of temperature?
questions.explanation: The kelvin uses the same step size as Celsius but starts at absolute zero, so 0 K = -273.15 degrees Celsius and kelvin values never go negative.
questions.memoryHook: Kelvin is the SI temperature unit.

questions.question: At what temperature does water freeze at sea level?
questions.explanation: At sea level, pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit); dissolving salt in the water lowers that freezing point.

questions.question: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
questions.explanation: At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius (212 degrees Fahrenheit); high on a mountain, lower air pressure makes it boil at a lower temperature.

questions.question: What are the three states of matter?
questions.explanation: Plasma is sometimes called a fourth state, found in stars and lightning, but the three everyday states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

questions.question: What is melting?
questions.correctAnswer: A solid changing into a liquid
distractors: A liquid changing into a gas
A gas changing into a liquid
A liquid changing into a solid
questions.explanation: Melting happens when a solid gains enough heat energy for its particles to break out of their fixed positions - ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.question: What is evaporation?
questions.correctAnswer: A liquid changing into a gas
distractors: A solid changing into a liquid
A gas changing into a liquid
A liquid changing into a solid
questions.explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature, as the fastest particles escape - it is how puddles dry up without boiling.

questions.question: What is condensation?
questions.correctAnswer: A gas changing into a liquid
distractors: A liquid changing into a gas
A solid changing into a liquid
A liquid changing into a solid
questions.explanation: Condensation is why dew forms on grass and a cold mirror fogs up: gas particles lose energy and clump together into liquid.

questions.question: What is freezing?
questions.correctAnswer: A liquid changing into a solid
distractors: A solid changing into a liquid
A gas changing into a liquid
A liquid changing into a gas
questions.explanation: Freezing is the reverse of melting: the liquid loses energy until its particles lock into fixed positions - for water, at 0 degrees Celsius.

questions.question: What is an atom?
questions.correctAnswer: The smallest unit of an element
questions.explanation: Atoms are far too small to see: millions of them side by side would span only the width of a full stop.

questions.question: What particles are in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explanation: The nucleus is the tiny, dense center of the atom; the electrons move in the space around it, not inside it.
questions.memoryHook: Protons and neutrons live in the nucleus.

questions.question: What is the charge of a proton?
questions.explanation: A proton carries a charge of +1, which exactly balances the -1 charge of one electron.

questions.question: What is the charge of an electron?
questions.explanation: An electron carries a charge of -1 and is far lighter than a proton - only about 1/1836 of a proton's mass.

questions.question: What is the charge of a neutron?
questions.explanation: Neutrons have almost the same mass as protons but carry no charge at all, which is why they are called neutral.

questions.question: What determines the identity of an element?
questions.explanation: Change the number of neutrons and you only get an isotope; change the number of protons and you have a completely different element.

questions.question: What is the atomic number?
questions.correctAnswer: The number of protons in an atom
distractors: The total of protons and neutrons
questions.explanation: The atomic number is printed in each element's box on the periodic table - carbon shows 6 because every carbon atom has 6 protons.

questions.question: What is the mass number?
questions.correctAnswer: The total of protons and neutrons
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, so its mass number is 12; electrons are not counted because their mass is almost zero.
questions.memoryHook: Mass number is protons plus neutrons.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for water?
questions.explanation: The formula is a recipe: H2O means every water molecule joins 2 hydrogen atoms to 1 oxygen atom - the small numbers count the atoms.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: CO2 means one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms; it is the gas you exhale and the gas plants take in.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for table salt?
questions.explanation: Table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen gas?
questions.explanation: Oxygen atoms travel in pairs, so the gas is written O2; a single O would mean one lone oxygen atom.

questions.question: What element has the symbol Fe?
questions.explanation: Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for iron - several symbols keep Latin names instead of matching the English word.

questions.question: What element has the symbol Au?
questions.explanation: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold, which is why this symbol does not match the English name at all.

questions.question: What element has the symbol Na?
questions.explanation: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name for sodium - like Fe for iron and Au for gold, the symbol keeps the older Latin root.

questions.question: What element has the symbol H?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is element number 1, the lightest element of all, with just one proton in its nucleus.

questions.question: What element has the symbol O?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is element number 8, with 8 protons, and it makes up about one fifth of the air you breathe.

questions.question: What element has the symbol C?
questions.explanation: Carbon is element number 6, the backbone of all known life; beware the look-alike symbols Ca (calcium), Cl (chlorine), and Cu (copper).

questions.question: What is a compound?
questions.correctAnswer: A substance made of two or more elements chemically joined
questions.explanation: In a compound the elements join in a fixed recipe - water is always 2 hydrogen to 1 oxygen - and the compound has properties unlike either element.

questions.question: What is a mixture?
questions.correctAnswer: Two or more substances mixed without chemical bonds
questions.explanation: A mixture keeps each substance's own properties and can be separated by physical means, like pulling iron filings out of sand with a magnet.

questions.question: What is a chemical change?
questions.correctAnswer: A change that makes a new substance
questions.explanation: Signs of a chemical change include gas bubbles forming, a color change, or heat and light given off - the original substances are used up.

questions.question: What is a physical change?
questions.correctAnswer: A change that does not make a new substance
distractors: A change that makes a new substance
questions.explanation: A physical change, like melting, makes no new substance.

questions.question: Which is an example of a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Burning wood reacts with oxygen and produces ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapor - new substances that were not there before.

questions.question: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
questions.explanation: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 with 7 in the middle; pure water is pH 7, neither acidic nor basic.

questions.question: What pH range is acidic?
questions.explanation: The lower the pH below 7, the more acidic the solution: lemon juice at about pH 2 is far more acidic than milk at about pH 6.

questions.question: What pH range is basic?
questions.explanation: The higher the pH above 7, the more basic the solution: soapy water and bleach sit near pH 12.

questions.question: What is an acid?
questions.correctAnswer: A substance that donates hydrogen ions and has pH below 7
questions.explanation: Donating hydrogen ions (H+) is what makes an acid act like an acid - the more H+ ions released, the lower the pH drops.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explanation: The ampere is named for Andre-Marie Ampere; one ampere means one coulomb of charge flows past a point every second.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of voltage?
questions.explanation: The volt is named for Alessandro Volta, who built an early battery; voltage measures how much energy each coulomb of charge carries.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of resistance?
questions.explanation: The ohm is named for Georg Ohm; one ohm of resistance lets a voltage of one volt push a current of exactly one ampere.

questions.question: What is Ohm's law?
questions.explanation: Use it as a working formula: a 12-volt battery connected across a 4-ohm resistor pushes a current of 12 / 4 = 3 amperes.

questions.question: What does a magnet attract?
questions.explanation: Magnets attract iron and similar metals.

questions.question: What are the poles of a magnet called?
questions.explanation: Every magnet has both poles - cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole.

questions.question: What happens when two north poles face each other?
questions.explanation: Opposite poles do the reverse: a north pole and a south pole pull toward each other and attract.

questions.question: What is density?
questions.explanation: Work it like this: a block with a mass of 50 grams and a volume of 10 cubic centimeters has a density of 50 / 10 = 5 grams per cubic centimeter.

questions.question: Which material is denser: water or oil?
questions.explanation: Oil floats on water because water is denser.
questions.memoryHook: Oil floats, so water is denser.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a series and a parallel circuit?
questions.correctAnswer: In series, current has one path; in parallel, it has many paths
distractors: In series, voltage is the same everywhere
In parallel, current is the same everywhere
questions.explanation: That is why one burnt-out bulb killed a whole string of old series-wired lights, while parallel house wiring lets every outlet work on its own.
questions.memoryHook: Series is one path, parallel is many.

questions.question: What is the center of an atom called?
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds nearly all the atom's mass in a tiny center - if an atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a marble in the middle.

questions.question: What is the periodic table organized by?
questions.explanation: The modern table orders elements by proton count, running from hydrogen (1) all the way to oganesson (118).
questions.memoryHook: The table is ordered by protons.

questions.question: What are the columns of the periodic table called?
questions.explanation: Elements stacked in one column behave alike chemically - Group 18, the noble gases, barely react with anything.

questions.question: What are the rows of the periodic table called?
questions.explanation: Moving across one period adds one proton and one electron at a time; starting a new row means starting a new electron shell.

questions.question: What gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 78 percent of air.
